forces: Trumpets, horns, oboes, bassoon, strings and continuo
performers: Marine Chamber Orchestra of the United States Marine Band; Major Michelle Rakers, conductor
question: What does a second hearing add to a short dance?
intro: The minuet that ends the programme is a tutti dance of only twenty-four bars in the score, in two strains each played twice. The recording then plays it through a second time, louder and without repeats.

sections.label: Second statement · first strain
sections.mNote: same strain, about five decibels louder

sections.label: Second statement · second strain
sections.mNote: second strain again, played once, louder

cues.title: Last piece in the programme
cues.text: Marking 300 years of the Water Music, the Marine Band’s concert of 29 January 2017 ends with this Minuet. Samuel Arnold’s 1788 full score also ends with it, marked Coro and followed by FINIS; modern editions number it 13, third in the suite.
cues.evidence: The programme’s running order ends with movement 13: https://web.archive.org/web/20251101025231id_/https://www.marineband.marines.mil/Portals/175/Docs/Programs/170129.pdf?ver=2017-01-24-094649-630 . The Marine Band’s announcement of 25 January 2017 says the concert celebrates the 300th anniversary of the Water Music: https://web.archive.org/web/20170219102546/http://www.marineband.marines.mil/News/Article/1060074/an-afternoon-of-water-music/ . Arnold’s score, pp. 52–53 (Coro, FINIS); HHA p. 50 (No. 13).

cues.title: Where the score rests the brass
cues.text: The first strain, played twice, has almost every instrument in the same rhythm. At about 0:36 the second strain begins. The score gives trumpets and horns three bars’ rest before they join at bar 12; the recording’s level shows no step at that point, so it cannot say whether they play.
cues.evidence: HHA bars 1–12 (p. 50): strain A, bars 1–8, has the whole orchestra in one rhythm; strain B, bars 9–24, has the trumpets and horns resting in bars 9–11 and entering in bar 12. The level differs by only −1.5 dB between bars 9–11 and bars 12–14 of the first hearing of the second strain (37.0–50.2 s) and by +0.5 dB in its repeat (71.4–84.6 s). The level dips to −27.0 dB at 36.08–36.20 s. A strain of 16 bars lasts about 35 s (2.18 s a bar). The official video shows players resting at times where the printed score gives them notes, so the printed parts are not assumed to sound.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The day on the river
cues.text: On 17 July 1717 about fifty musicians played on a barge beside George I’s. Friedrich Bonet reported that the Prince of Wales and his wife were conspicuously absent. Father and son were quarrelling; in November 1717 a quarrel ended with the Prince ejected from the king’s palace.
cues.evidence: Bonet’s diary entry and the dispute, as given in Robert King’s note for Hyperion CDA66967: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA66967

cues.title: The whole Minuet again, louder
cues.text: After a gap of about 0.3 seconds the minuet starts again from bar 1 and runs through once without repeats, about five decibels louder than before. Around 2:10, in score bar 12, the level rises about four decibels more, a step the first statement does not show at the same bar.
cues.evidence: The relative level falls to −34.3 dB at 105.7–106.0 s. The mean level of the second statement’s first strain is 5.4 dB above that of the two hearings of the first strain; in its second strain the level is 3.9 dB higher in bars 12–14 (about 130–137 s) than in bars 9–11, against −1.5 and +0.5 dB in the first statement. The printed notes are the same.

cues.title: No autograph survives
cues.text: No autograph score of the Water Music survives. John Walsh printed parts for about half of the movements in the 1730s, and Samuel Arnold published the first full score in 1788, which ends with this Minuet. The grouping into three suites appears to date from the 1950s.
cues.evidence: Robert King’s note for Hyperion CDA66967 (no autograph; Walsh’s parts held only about half the movements; Arnold’s full score of 1788): https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA66967 . IMSLP credits Thurston Dart with the three-suite designation in the 1950s, first published by Eulenburg in 1959: https://imslp.org/wiki/Water_Music,_HWV_348-350_(Handel,_George_Frideric) . Arnold’s score ends with this movement, p. 53 (FINIS).

cues.title: The last chord, then silence
cues.text: The last chord ends at about 2:40 and four seconds of near silence follow. Then bright, steady sound at about −14 dB begins and lasts about half a minute; the video shows the players standing and the audience in silhouette, consistent with applause.
cues.evidence: The relative level is −12.0 dB at 159 s, −15.7 dB at 160 s and −40.0 dB at 161 s, stays near −38 to −44 dB until 163.5 s, is −24.6 dB at 164 s and between −12 and −16 dB from 165 s to about 194 s, then fades (−27.7 dB at 195 s). The tail is bright (spectral centroid about 2.4–2.5 kHz). The official video’s frames over the last half-minute show the whole orchestra standing and silhouettes at the lower edge of the picture.

transitions.title: The second strain begins
transitions.how: The first strain ends on a held D major chord, a dotted minim in every part, and its repeat sign is taken once. The second strain begins at bar 9; the score gives trumpets and horns three bars’ rest and brings them in at bar 12. The recording dips to about −27 dB for 0.1 seconds at the join. Its level shows no step at bar 12, so the level alone does not show whether the brass play in this first statement.
transitions.evidence: The relative level dips to −27.0 dB at 36.08–36.20 s. HHA bars 7–12 (printed p. 50) and Arnold’s 1788 score, pp. 52–53, where the first strain ends with a repeat sign and the trumpet and horn staves are empty at the start of the next system. The level is −25.6 dB in bars 9–11 and −27.1 dB in bars 12–14 of the second strain’s first hearing.

transitions.title: A pause, then the Minuet again, louder
transitions.how: The second strain’s repeat ends and the recording falls to about −34 dB for 0.3 seconds. The orchestra then starts again from bar 1 and plays the twenty-four bars once, without repeats. The level is about five decibels higher than in either hearing of the first strain, though the printed notes are the same; the recording does not show how the extra weight is made.
transitions.evidence: The relative level falls to −34.3 dB at 105.7–106.0 s. The mean level of 106.3–123 s is 5.4 dB above that of 3–18.5 s and 19.5–36 s.

transitions.title: Bar 12 brings a louder step
transitions.how: The first strain ends on its held chord and the second begins at bar 9, where the score gives trumpets and horns three bars’ rest before their entry at bar 12. This time the recording’s level rises about four decibels at bar 12, around 2:10, and the strain is played once, without its repeat, ending at about 2:40 on a held D major chord. The recording does not show which instruments account for the rise.
transitions.evidence: HHA bars 9–12 (printed p. 50). The level is 3.9 dB higher in the second statement’s bars 12–14 than in its bars 9–11, against −1.5 and +0.5 dB in the first statement’s two hearings of the strain. Strain boundaries from the dips at 105.9 s and about 123 s.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Marine Chamber Orchestra, United States Marine Band (orchestra), Major Michelle A. Rakers (conductor)
fields.note: Commons gives the conductor as Major Michelle Rakers; the programme prints Major Michelle A. Rakers. No roster of individual players is published in the consulted sources. The video’s closing frames show the whole orchestra standing; the ensemble’s harpsichord, bassoon and trumpet are visible in the other movements’ videos, and no frame shows horns or oboes. Which sections play in each statement is not established: an independent look at the official video reports upper-string players resting at about 1:05, where the printed score gives them notes, so the recording is not assumed to follow the printed parts. No orchestra view is authored for this movement for that reason.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Performing edition not identified. The movement number (13 of the three suites) and the strains heard (a first strain of 8 bars and a second of 16, each played twice) match the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe text. The recording then plays all 24 bars once more without repeats, which that edition does not print; no editor or continuo realisation is credited.
fields.note: The programme and Commons name the work and movement numbers but no edition. The Hallische Händel-Ausgabe (Redlich, 1962) prints 24 bars with a repeat sign after bar 8 and after bar 24 and no da capo; the second statement follows from the measured pauses (about 54 s for 24 bars at the first statement’s pace) and is a feature of this performance. Commons and the candidate list place this movement fifth in the suite; the edition numbers it third (13), and Arnold’s 1788 score prints it last, headed Coro.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Commons gives performance_date 2017-01-29; the programme prints Sunday, January 29, 2017 at 2:00 P.M.; the official video description repeats the date. This Minuet is the last item of the programme. The Commons composition_date field, 1717-07-17, is the date of the documented first performance on the Thames, not a composition date.

fields.note: No transfer date is documented. The YouTube publication date (30 April 2018) and the Commons upload date (28 June 2021) are not session or transfer dates.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Opus audio file (48 kHz, two channels, encoder Lavf58.29.100) listed on Commons with the Marine Band’s YouTube playlist as its source; Commons supplies an MP3 access derivative. The file keeps the audience’s applause after the last chord.
fields.note: The file’s own metadata documents the Opus format and encoder. That the audio was taken from the official video’s sound track is inferred from the source field and from the matching title and duration (195 s); the processing chain is not described. That the closing half-minute is applause is inferred from its sound and from the standing players and audience silhouettes in the video’s last frames.

fields.value: Handel (died 1759): the composition is in the public domain.
fields.note: Commons tags the composition PD-old-auto-expired (death year 1759). The performing edition is not identified; editorial copyright in a modern edition, if one was used, is separate from the sound recording.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Commons tags the performance and recording PD-USGov-Military-Marines: a work of a United States Marine or employee made as part of official duties, public domain as a work of the U.S. federal government.
fields.note: This is a U.S.-jurisdiction statement, not a claim of worldwide status. The programme carries a general notice that a performance may contain third-party material and should not be assumed to be public domain; no third-party material is identified in this performance of a composition from before 1759, but the notice is recorded here. The official Marine Band YouTube channel published the source video.

composer.epithet: A German-trained composer of Italian opera who made the English chorus an actor in public musical drama.
facts: With Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow in Halle; theatre work in Hamburg; study and commissions in Italy, 1706–10
Hanover briefly; settled in London in 1712; became a British subject in 1727
Italian operas, English oratorios, anthems, concertos, chamber cantatas and ceremonial orchestral music
composer.background:
Handel grew up in Halle, the son of a barber-surgeon, and studied with Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow, organist of the town’s principal church. Zachow’s teaching included counterpoint, keyboard playing and the copying of other composers’ music. Handel briefly enrolled at the university and held an organist’s post before moving to Hamburg in 1703. Its public opera house offered a different education: he played in the orchestra and encountered the practical demands of singers, stage machinery and mixed theatrical repertory. His first opera, Almira, was performed there in 1705, with a German text incorporating Italian arias.

From 1706 to 1710 Handel worked in Italy, writing cantatas, sacred music and opera for patrons in Florence, Rome, Naples and Venice. Rome gave him access to virtuoso singers and to instrumentalists associated with Corelli. The Latin Dixit Dominus of 1707 demands rapid, independent choral lines and sustained control of dissonance; the chamber cantatas make emotional turns within much smaller forces. Agrippina, performed in Venice at the end of 1709, assembles much previously written material into a calculated theatrical comedy. Reuse was already part of his method: a successful musical gesture could acquire a different function when assigned to a new character and situation.
